Field of Dreams

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
we follow Lee den Hond on the toughest footrace on Earth

Unique Selling Point:
Four years ago we followed local adventurer Lee to the top of the world when she became the 3rd South African woman to summit Mount Everest. Now we follow in her footsteps as she crosses the Sahara Desert in the formidably challenging Marathon des Sables in Morocco.

Summary:
In 2013 Carte Blanche viewers opened their hearts and wallets to support Lee's climb, and her quest to improve the plight of hundreds of children in the Schaumberg informal settlement near Hartebeespoort Dam. Her vision was to build a Children's Centre where all the children of the community would have a place to play and learn. Today the Centre stands proud on 9 hectares of land known as the Field of Dreams. Not only is this a place for the children, but for the entire community. The surrounding land is used to grow vegetables, host sporting matches, and the Centre is used for literacy classes, skills transfer and a clinic.

Further information:
Lee recently ran the gruellling Marathon des Sables (250km over 5 days 50 degrees) to raise money for her latest dream - the Field of Dreams Children's Clinic. Architects have already been engaged to design a dedicated clinic that will be built on the grounds to cater to the health challenges faced by the most vulnerable in our community.

Script:


FIELD OF DREAMS

V/O: This is the Sahara Desert – vast, uncompromising, hot. This particular patch of hell is in Morocco, 7 hours from the closest town. It’s the venue for the 32nd running of an ultra-marathon that is known as the toughest foot race on earth – the Marathon des Sables. The buses arrive in the middle of nowhere, carrying endurance athletes representing 52 countries, including South Africa. The 6 men and 2 women will be sharing accommodation – an open-sided, traditional Berber tent made from goat’s hair. Among them is Lee den Hond.

Lee: In terms of your kit you’ve got essentially one outfit for the week; you’ve got two pairs of socks, two pairs of shorts, two T-shirts. I’m going to be smelling really good at the end of it, and minimal toiletries. And essentially, most important is your nutrition, and what you’re drinking. Every single day we get 10 litres of water, the big say we’re getting 22 litres, essentially very minimalistic and we’re travelling light.

V/O: Lee lined up to hand in her main suitcase and have her race pack weighed. What she thought was 8kg, turned out be 12. This is what she’ll be carrying on her back for the next 6 days

Lee: They’ve checked passports, they’ve explained the salt tablets: we’ve got to take 2 salt tablets per litre of water for the next 7 days; ECG was checked, we’re good to go.

V/O: Carte Blanche first met Lee in 2013, on the first step of an extraordinary journey. Her goal was to climb Mount Everest and raise funds for the children of Schaumburg, an informal settlement near Hartesbeespoort Dam. She invited the children to sign the South African flag that she would carry to the top of the world.

Lee: I want to appeal to every single South African to climb this mountain with me. I want to raise the money, and I want them to raise money towards these children to build an orphanage, a centre and a clinic to better their lives, so one day they can believe they can climb Everest, their own Everest.

V/O: In April 2013, we flew to Nepal and trekked with her to Everest Base Camp. Through the villages clinging to mountain-sides. Over the suspension bridges, swaying above the icy water.
Up, up into the Himalayas, battling the cold and the high altitude, passing the peaks that tower over the Earth.

Lee: I feel so committed to this flag, so committed to the children - the spirit of the children - to go to the top of the word and to make this dream come true.

V/O: Lee became the third South African woman to successfully summit Mount Everest, and flew the flag she had faithfully carried with her. Inspired by her quest, Carte Blanche viewers and corporate donors opened their hearts and wallets. R834 000 was raised towards her vision for Schaumburg.

Jonas: She came back, she said “Jonas I’m back, we’re going to implement my plans.” We sat down with the committee, she do it exactly the way we asked.

V/O: Jonas Ndou is the Chairperson of the Schaumburg Residents Committee.

Jonas: There were schools but you know they need papers. A lot of the kids here they didn’t have papers. A lot of the parents, they’re coming from outside of the country.

V/O: In 2014 she purchased a piece of land over the road from Schaumburg, and called it the Field of Dreams.

Lee: We designed the Centre, and we got the ball rolling in terms of building. And what was really great Bongani, is that the people who actually built the Centre were all builders and labourers from the Schaumberg community. It was very important that these people were building a Centre for their children and for their Community.

Link: Four years ago, this was just an idea; and here is the vision made real. The Field of Dreams – a children’s Centre where anything is possible.




Lee: So, the children come here three days a week, they come at 7.30 in the morning, they leave at 1.30, they’re fed twice day. We’ve got 3 amazing women that prepare the food, who work in the kitchen. We’ve also got a team of gardening people to ensure that the grounds, and also the vegetables are also supplied to the kitchen to feed the children three times per week.

V/O: There is a small library and a computer centre with educational programs. The facilitators who take care of the children are also residents of Schaumburg, and are trained on a weekly basis by the Head of Operations, social worker Example Valoyi.

Example: The Centre for the community provides hope, it provides a sense of ownership. It makes them believe that there is a future.

V/O: And it’s this ability to dream big that allows her to achieve the impossible. It’s Day 1 of the desert marathon. What lies ahead is the stuff of legend: a grueling multi-stage adventure through a mythical landscape in one of the world’s most inhospitable environments.  Over eleven hundred athletes kick off at the Start. The first day is the shortest distance: only 30km, but in temperatures above 40 degrees. At the back of the field is the sweeper vehicle – a camel. There’s no road or laid out route, but after 18km Lee arrives at the first checkpoint.

Lee: This pack, pack on my back – 10k’s, not good at all. Sore shoulder, I’ve got to lose some of the load tonight. I think it’s a bit like life, you’ve got to lighten the load big time. Alright so this is Day 1 packed lunch: biltong, true South African, dried fruit.

V/O: After lunch and another 12 k’s, they reached the bivouac point for the night. Lee had a chance to catch her breath and reflect on the day.

Lee: Today was a gentle day, tomorrow is meant to be really, really tough with a lot of sand dunes. There are disabled athletes, there are blind runners doing it, there’s a special needs child of ten-years-old being pushed by a French team. There’s so many reasons to feel amazing about being part of such a special event.

V/O: Day 2 didn’t disappoint - the dunes went up in size and so did the temperature.

Lee: And then in the middle of nowhere at about the 35km mark was this mountain – a very steep, rocky incline which went up about a kilometre in height - then a very steep decline which was just sand coming all the way down, and then it was a home run.

V/O: And by Day 3, things just got worse. Even though the distance was a bit shorter, conditions had intensified, with temperatures reaching fifty-three degrees.

Lee: Those hills were quite brutal and the heat is very intense today, and there’s no wind. It’s a big difference.

V/O: But Day 4 is the biggest challenge. This stage is 87km, almost the equivalent of the Comrades marathon – and Lee’s feet are suffering.

Lee: We had 67 paramedics supporting the race. On Day 1 no athletes had blisters, by Day 3 they were treating over 7000 blisters.

Lee: You know why! Hi guys….

V/O And the going just got tougher. Mile after mile, hour after hour, but she managed to keep her spirits up. By sunset the runners have only reached halfway. They will run through the night, guided only by their headlamps and hope they don’t encounter any desert vipers or scorpions.

Lee: You’ve got to focus on every single foot in front of you. This headlight is completely key even though it’s a magnificent full moon, and I’ve got a very long night ahead.

V/O: Lee finished that stage the next morning, 23 hours after she started.

Lee: So happy it’s behind me, so happy. So hard, hard, hard, hard. So much sand!

V/O: The final day dawns and everyone is exhausted. This stage is the length of a full marathon, but Lee is full of energy. In her backpack is the South African flag signed by the children, the same flag she took to the top of Mount Everest.

Lee: It was unbelievably important to finish the race again with the South African flag. It is about the children, what the flag symbolises, what it represents. There are so many reasons to finish things in life.
